city-digital-twin · Newcastle study · project report

Built and measured, read by a fixed instrument, and every control still unrun

2026-09-14HEAD b8f89ffbranch praneetdhoolia/docs-home-viewer-and-tenth-reportgate PASS (19 of 19)

The tenth reading of the project finds it BUILT AND MEASURED - arm 0 of F35 executed its 300-iteration horizon in 30.35 h, the project's second RESULT, and reads car +9.6 % and motorbike -5.6 % inside the goal's 10 % band with six modes past the 20 % stop bar - and finds that what moved the scoreboard since the first result was the footpath rebuild and the engines' routing, not any of the controls the reports asked for: every model-side control (the raptor mode cost, MSA at the cutoff, random plan removal, service quality, pt submode alternatives) is built and unrun, and ride's target sits above the coverage the demand seeds. This session moved the documents to docs/, cut the framing documents to what a reader needs, rebuilt the run viewer so the twelve modes are read against their targets live on a street map or imagery, and worked four of the ninth report's five code issues (#197-#200); the code lane finds 4 defects, 22 risks and 31 smells at HEAD - two of the defects in the viewer built today (a process-global stdout redirect and a shared module global in the in-process reading) and one in the second result's close-out, whose findings never reached results/processed. The field is unchanged: 55 agent-based city projects on 12 platforms, the per-mode-ridership rung empty everywhere but here, and the nearest like-for-like clock (Kelheim's 25 % at ~139 s an iteration for a fifth of the population) says the 346 s iteration is the physics of 2.3 million walk legs on 383,000 links, not our code, which is 4-5 % of it and falling. The next thing that can move a mode is a pair arm - the routers pair first - or the demand rebuild that seeds ride at its share; nothing on this page is a result until one of them runs.

Method

Six lanes in parallel, one agent each, on HEAD b8f89ff (the session branch, eight commits past the PR #201 merge, tree clean): a code reviewer over six areas reading the code_metrics rows first; a performance analyst over performance.json, arm 0's stopwatch and gc.log; a historian over every PR body, the commit log and the timeline; a document reviewer over every living document, hook, workflow and skill with a relative-link check; a field researcher and a factor researcher starting from the reference library and spending 40 and 35 calls on its gaps. The mechanical half came from the three collectors (metrics.json, code_metrics.json, performance.json). Ratings 1-5 per area and dimension, each with two pieces of evidence, never averaged across areas. The synthesis re-read twelve cited file:lines and re-fetched five sources searched this pass.

The timeline from day 0

  • 10 Aug: the whole package, network and demand land in one day (PRs #1-#3); the next morning nothing loads (PR #4) and P4 begins with the cost of a run measured.
  • 11-16 Aug: one 73-commit PR (#38) declares every value in a registry, splits the city from the framework, and rebuilds the network after the harvest box was found clipping 87 SA1s; the first arms run (F1).
  • 18-21 Aug: ride pairing is built and found starved (0.104 % pairable); every person-transport mode becomes physical in a stacked set of PRs that strands five of them (#56); the direct-commit ban and the F4 arms (67 h each) follow.
  • 24-25 Aug: C5 exists off arm A; the project is renamed; SUMO is descoped and the all-modes batch (signals, crossings, dwell, taxi) is built inert then activated as F6; the first gate fires and the documents are pinned to their artefacts.
  • 26-29 Aug: the gate loop runs a family a day (F7-F13): the ride ratchet, escort coherence, the declared-pair identity, taxi physical, SCATS, the taxi fleet; the yardsticks themselves are found wrong (another city's stop; truck on the wrong basis).
  • 30 Aug: the busiest day - 87 commits, 31 record rows, families F14-F21, the demand rebuilt on measured licence rates, and the record frozen behind GOAL.md, a one-page board and thirteen position pages (#101).
  • 31 Aug-2 Sep: fares priced (bus inside at a gate for the first time), the results store, bike stress / parking search / income (F23), and the 25 %-only directive.
  • 3-5 Sep: requirement 10 and the issue gate; the first project report and its 26 issues closed without a run; destinations balanced; a unit-test layer; a stopped run becomes citable.
  • 6-8 Sep: car inside at the F28 gate (+6.6 %); four reports in one day; the holdout breach fixed; the iteration profiled (310 -> 205 s); the objective restated to the twelve modes and the search made runnable; F31 gate car +5.4 %.
  • 9-10 Sep: the first result since F4 (F32, 300 iterations, 21.5 h) - relaxing makes the fit worse (0 of 12); the counts rung was on the wrong roads for 25 days; ride's target is above its choice-set coverage; F33's arm dies of a heap nobody set.
  • 11-12 Sep: the launcher refuses what killed arm 0; the footpath network rebuild (F34) doubles the iteration and F35's engines recover 17 %; arm 0 launches on a measured price.
  • 13-14 Sep: arm 0 lands as the second result (2 of 12 inside: car +9.6 %, motorbike -5.6 %); the reader that read heavy rail 0 is fixed; the horizon is declared 250; the documents move to docs/ and the tenth report is lodged with no arm running.

Three questions

could_it_be_simpler
Yes, in five places that are also where the findings cluster: (1) the four binder passes and write_day in the demand build, which repeat one frame and stream the same CSVs (a Binder abstraction and one stream: ~1,500 lines); (2) the reporter, which computes and prints through a module global that the viewer, --trend and the gate watcher then read back - returning the reading would remove both viewer defects; (3) run()'s three terminal branches beside close_out; (4) the eighteen acquisition adapters and their three copies of one rule; (5) the 2,820 lines of Java config-group accessors that duplicate param_config.json. Retaining every function, the six areas could lose roughly 9,000 of 76,000 lines without a behaviour change, and every one of those cuts removes a place where two copies of one thing can disagree - which is the defect class the ninth and tenth reports keep finding.
is_the_reader_honest_about_results
Yes at every gate that matters: fit, the figures, the calibration report, the board, the run index, resume matching and the calibrated base all test completion == ran_to_last_iteration, a stopped arm is cited at the record's reached_iteration and never past it, the running arm's iteration is printed as 'live', and the pre-pandemic patronage stays unscored. Three honesty gaps remain: ferry receives a deviation and a STOP flag against a derived target whose sweep spans zero while the reader's own docstring says it does not; every reading resolves residents through today's population file rather than the run's own; and the viewer's in-process reading can attach one run's rows to another's iteration under concurrent requests and cache the result.
what_no_check_sees
A numeric literal inside an expression assigned to an ALL-CAPS name (six sites, two of them registry copies and one a sweep); a registry value re-typed in a dict(...) call; whether a build-stage field moves any artefact (reach is proven only for config fields); which checkout the interpreter's .pth points at before a build runs; a gate milestone the watcher let go; the holdout as a file rather than a label; an absolute machine path in a generated reference document; two cities writing one docs/; the viewer's memory inside the harness process; and the difference between a local gate list and CI's.

architecture
The build layer is a chain of stand-alone scripts, each reading the registry at import (CFG = registry.load()) and the city's artefacts through city.path(), and each writing a report JSON beside its outputs. Every draw is seeded from B.seed.master or a blake2b hash of the household id (build_activity_chains.py:275-279), and no build script reads the wall clock except the manifest's generated stamp and the timing wrapper. The demand chain is B1 (population) -> B2 (tours, then four binder passes that each read and rewrite the day file) -> plans (two streams of the first-day CSV, then write_day per day type) -> run inputs (six gzip passes over the network per scenario x day). The five #198 fields landed as declared: P_INTERMEDIATE_STOP_DEFAULT, STOP_SHOP_SHARE and DECAY_TARGET_DEFAULT_KM in build_activity_chains.py:194-195/:325 and the two city defaults in build_corridor_road_attributes.py:156 and build_landuse_parking.py:340. The layer's weak point is not randomness or wall-clock (both clean) but duplicated numbers: registry values re-typed in the same layer that also reads them, in forms the hardcoding gate cannot see.

testability
Low. The builders are module-level scripts that load the registry and open city files at import (build_population.py:35, build_activity_chains.py CFG at import), so a unit test cannot import one without the package present; 0 of the 39 build modules is imported by a unit test (code_metrics tests.uncovered_src_modules lists build_population, build_activity_chains, build_matsim_plans, build_matsim_network, build_network_layers, build_params, build_zone_attractions). The determinism claims are testable only by a full rebuild and a byte diff, which tests/check_package.py does locally. What is testable today: the pure helpers (age_sex_dist, lf_rates_from, income_band_midpoint, sample_unit_hash) - none has a test.

architecture
run.py resolves the registry through overlays, runs a preflight that re-emits the config into a temp dir, then either registers a Task Scheduler one-shot (--detach) or calls run_matsim.run(). run() reconciles stale cards, prices the arm, refuses a small heap, a missing automatic stop, unsafe telemetry and (new since the ninth report) a concurrent arm, names the directory by launch stamp, writes _meta.json, starts the JVM and three daemon watchers (gate every N iterations via the reporter subprocess, wall ceiling, log-silence stall), plus the in-process live viewer and the progress digest. A stop of any kind writes a marker before the JVM dies; the survivor of the race (harness or --stop) reads the marker, calls mark_dead (rename to aborted_) and close_out (record, summary, mirror into processed, trim). results_store owns every path under results/ and is the only deleter; procs owns liveness. Log readers are bounded: run_failure reads a 64 MiB tail, the iteration readers go through the progress digest first and the incremental offset cache second, and iteration_times falls back to a full sequential read only when both are absent.

testability
Medium, and the best in the repository: results_store, run_matsim's watchers and close-out, run_failure, procs and issue_gate are covered by 20 of the 53 unit test files (test_close_out, test_stop_run, test_trim_grace, test_ceiling_watch, test_heap_rule_and_stall_watch, test_find_completed, test_refuse_concurrent_arm, test_incremental_log_read, ...), and tests/check_gate_watcher.py drives the watcher with a fake JVM. Not covered: run.py itself (a module-level argparse main), _detach, install_paths' persistence path, the give-up branch of the gate loop, and reconcile_stale's log-first ordering. The functions are testable because the watchers take proc and cfg as arguments and the readers are pure over a directory.

architecture
One reader owns each question: iteration_reading decodes a trips or legs table once per process (bounded to six tables), extract_metrics owns the finished-run metrics and the run's own schedule (fixed in PR #201), report_mode_ridership scores the twelve modes per iteration and writes the gate verdict that the runner now appends to _readings.jsonl, fit.py scores a run against the calibration split and stamps completion and is_a_result, calibrate.py searches candidates it assembles into the committed set and restores in a finally, and the board, the run index, the fit figures and the calibration report all gate on completion == ran_to_last_iteration. The viewer is a threading HTTP server that runs INSIDE the harness process for a live run (run_matsim.start_live_view) and stand-alone otherwise; it serves the incremental log reader, the modes ledger (stored readings first, an in-process report() on a thread when a requested iteration has none), a per-run reprojected network cache and the congestion window as packed binary, and the page draws with Leaflet from cdnjs plus OSM/Esri tiles when online and a built-in projection when not.
findings
severityfilelinesummaryfailure_scenario
defectsrc/analyse/run_view.py524_compute_reading runs report() under contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf) on a daemon thread; sys.stdout is process-global, and for a live run this server lives in the HARNESS process (run_matsim.py:955-957, background=True). While a reading computes - a 25 % trips table decode, tens of seconds to minutes - every harness print (gate watcher verdicts, the ceiling and stall stop lines, mark_dead's rename report) is captured into the StringIO and discarded; two readings in flight (_start_reading dedupes only the same key, :539-553) restore sys.stdout out of order and leave it bound to a finished buffer for the rest of the run.A person opens the live view of a detached 44 h arm and clicks two iterations; from that moment results/_launch/<task>.log - the only record of a detached arm - stops receiving the gate watcher's 'stopping the run at iteration 200' line and the stall watcher's cause, and the record's cause text is reconstructed from the log tail instead.
defectsrc/analyse/run_view.py530_compute_reading reads rmr.LAST after report() returns; LAST is one module-level dict that every report() call rewrites (report_mode_ridership.py:486-494, :548-551 append rows during printing). Two readings computing at once (a second iteration, or a second run from the picker) interleave their writes, so the reading cached under (run A, it 100) can carry run B's rows, fraction and source, and _MODES_CACHE keeps it for the life of the server.The page's scoreboard shows iteration 100 of arm 0 with the twelve rows of the 1 % smoke probe picked in another tab, labelled as arm 0, and the trend sparkline draws a jump nobody can reproduce.
risksrc/analyse/run_view.py597_NET_CACHE is keyed by run_dir, never evicted and never locked under ThreadingMixIn: one 368,230-link network costs about 131 MB of Python objects (measured with a same-shape proxy), the same input network is parsed and held once per run the picker visits rather than once per path, and two concurrent first requests parse the gzip twice; _BASEMAP_CACHE is unlocked the same way.A viewer left open across a session's six runs holds ~0.8 GB of geometry inside the harness process that also carries the 48 GB JVM's child on a 63 GB host.
risksrc/analyse/run_view.py516The reading is computed in-process: rmr.report decodes the iteration's trips and legs tables through iteration_reading.table (:41 CACHE_TABLES = 6, bounded by count not bytes) inside whichever process serves the page - for a live run, the harness.At 25 % a trips table decodes to roughly a gigabyte of dict rows; six of them plus the network cache put the harness at several GB beside a 48 GB heap, which is the #66 swap-stall class the stall watcher was written for - triggered by a click on the page.

architecture
The contract has three tiers. The portable schemas under config/schema declare what any city must supply; required_fields.json and layers.json are GENERATED from the reference city's registry and checked current in CI, and the output schemas inject the active city's scenario and day vocabulary at validation time (outputs.py:63-80) so the files themselves stay city-free. The registry resolver validates every field (intrinsic rules, jsonschema when importable) on every load() and range-checks overlay values leaf by leaf since #200. check_hardcoding is the ledger of decided values in four scanners (string-literal key reach, legacy-constant AST scan, coordinate scan, inline-literal scan) with a STRUCTURAL/STRUCTURAL_INLINE exception list of 41 + 75 entries. CI runs nine jobs offline: compile, the three check_*.py scripts, unit tests, manifest, doc currency and shape, the city contract, zero hardcoding, a fixture second city, and provenance JSON validity. Locally, session_gate runs a similar but not identical list. check_package.py (2,091 lines, module-level) is the only executable test of the built package and runs on a workstation only.

architecture
Eighteen adapters, each a script with its own download loop, sha256 helper and provenance writer, produce raw files under data/raw that the manifest hashes and the build layer reads. The retrieval-date rule (#199) is now one rule stated three times: a fetched file is stamped today, a held file keeps its recorded date, and a held file with no record takes its mtime and says so in retrieved_basis. Provenance comes in two shapes - a list of per-file records (abs_dem, licences, open_data, speed_zones, gtfs) and a dict with a top-level licence and a files array (boam, opal_patronage, osm, fares, osm_attic, p2p, planning_tia) - and the manifest builder reads both. Extents come from the dissolved LGA boundary (overpass.py docstring) rather than typed rectangles; the CRS is read from city.json in most adapters but typed in two. The sandbox allowlist now covers every host a provenance record names (test_provenance_hosts_allowed, 10 hosts across the manifest's 959 source_url cells). Validation targets are split calibration/holdout by row label in one CSV that every reader opens whole.

architecture
CitysimControler assembles nineteen config groups and the modules over a stock MATSim controler: the ride pairing engine (BeforeMobsim pairs declared and inferred passengers with drivers, routes the driver's detour on a worker pool and - since #197 - writes the plan on the main thread in driver order), the joint-ride qsim engine (a booked passenger physically boards the driver's car, waits at the meeting point under the booking's window and times out onto the Tier-1 clock), the taxi fleet engine, the generic route teleporter, the gated subtour mode choice (reach, mixed-subtour, bound-role and permissibility gates that restore the pre-innovation plan on refusal), the escort coherence listener (a seeded per-iteration Random), the household vehicle roster, the fare/parking/crowding/service-quality/bike-stress scoring handlers, and RunTelemetry, which documents that it has no thread safety of its own and relies on the sim-step barrier the registry declares and a test pins. The signals stack is a separate Maven build. Randomness is seeded everywhere it appears; the wall clock is read only for timing logs; the only id-suffix parse is ParkingChargeHandler's activity type split and JointRideEngine's fallback vehicle id.

testability
Low in the Java itself: there is no JUnit suite; the probes (GatedSubtourProbe, RemodeRestoreProbe, PtFareProbe, GradientTableProbe, NestedSubtourProbe, SubtourChainScan, the three signals probes) are main() programs run by hand, and the Python unit tests pin the contract from outside (test_telemetry_barrier, test_direct_walk_counters, test_raptor_mode_cost, test_pt_submode_choice, test_service_quality, test_plan_removal_one_selector read the Java source as text). The engines take the scenario and the qsim, so a JUnit test over a ten-agent scenario is possible and would cover the wait-timeout and the detour-apply paths that today only a 25 % arm exercises.

how_they_moved_between_families
F32 -> F35 (road graph -> footpath network + engines route their re-modes)
iteration 243.5 -> 346.5 s (+42 %): mobsim 193 -> 236 s (+22 % for 4.5x the departures: 623k -> 2.80 M, of which 2.30 M are walk legs the qsim now executes at PCE 0), replanning 25 -> 85 s (+240 %, the router on 363,818 walk links against 200,935 car links; F34 probe read 130 s on the same graph, arm 0 fell to 84 by it.101+), prepareForMobsim 26 -> 2 s (the null-route whole-plan re-route of 9.168 removed), beforeMobsimListeners 4 -> 17 s (the refused-taxi walks now routed by the engine, 47.6 s at it.0 falling to 1.3 s at it.300 as refusals fell 45,573 -> 2,063; RidePairingEngine 6.5 -> 10.2-11.7 s per ride_pairing.csv elapsed_ms)
F34 probe -> F35 probe (same network, the 9.168 Java change)
555.5 -> 460.0 s recurring (-17 %): prepareForMobsim 92 -> 2, mobsim 328 -> 262, replanning 130 unchanged, beforeMobsim 13.5 -> 70.5 (the work moved, then shrank on the arm as refusals fell)
within arm 0
the pace FELL 397 (it.2-24) -> 367 (it.26-99) -> 343 s (it.101-239) -> 262 s tail: replanning 110 -> 84 and beforeMobsim 46 -> 16 track the taxi refusal count (45,573 -> 6,339 by it.200) and the shrinking re-route load; the mobsim was flat at 232-237 s throughout
our_listeners_named
beforeMobsimListeners order (matsim.log it.0)
EventsHandlingImpl (opens the events writer on dump iterations) -> PlansDumpingImpl ('dump all plans', 199 s on 13 iterations) -> VspPlansCleaner -> citysim.TaxiFleetEngine -> citysim.RidePairingEngine
TaxiFleetEngine.notifyBeforeMobsim (TaxiFleetEngine.java:198-256)
per iteration: collect() walks every selected plan's trips (one getLegsOnly per trip), sorts requests, simulates the 200-vehicle fleet on a PriorityQueue, then remodeRefused() routes every refused trip as a network walk on global.numberOfThreads=20 workers via RemodeRestore.route. Measured on arm 0 (grep 'routed as a network walk'): 45,573 walks in 47.6 s (it.0), 47,798 in 53.4 s (it.2), 28,447 in 29.9 s (it.24), 8,643 in 6.6 s (it.99), 6,339 in 5.6 s (it.199), 2,063 in 1.3 s (it.300) - ~1.0-1.1 ms per routed walk on 20 threads

hoistable
RemodeRestore.route (RemodeRestore.java:173-215) builds Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers) and calls routers.get() once per worker on EVERY call - twice an iteration (taxi, ride) plus routeDetoursInParallel's own pool (:1234): three pools and up to 60 TripRouters per iteration. The engine's own comment (:948-956) says the NUMBER of routers built is part of the random sequence (RandomizingTimeDistanceTravelDisutility draws on construction), so hoisting the routers is a family boundary by design, not a free change; the pools alone are hoistable; the wall cost is not separable at 1 s stopwatch resolution (the it.300 pass: 2,063 walks in 1.3 s including pool + router setup)

pace_vs_fraction
docs/positions/sampling-and-families.md states NO pace law - it states that 1 % is unusable for results (flow-capacity granularity), that fraction sensitivity flattens from 10 % to 25 %, and that the 10-25 % threshold is unmeasured (lines 64, 78). What the runs say: on one build (F1) 10 % -> 25 % was 33.3 -> 90.2 s (2.7x for 2.5x agents); on the F35 build 1 % -> 25 % is 50.4-51.0 -> 346 s (6.8x for 25x agents, at 8 vs 16 qsim threads): the mobsim 32.5 -> 236 s (7.3x), replanning 4 -> 85 s (21x, near-linear per agent), beforeMobsim 6 -> 17 s. The fixed part (2,139 transit vehicles simulated at any fraction, a 382k-link network, 20 min of setup routing at 25 % vs ~1.4 min at 1 %) makes the per-agent cost fall with fraction, so pace is sub-linear in fraction, while 9.168 measured the footpath network's cost as super-linear in agents x graph (+35 % at 1 %, +88 % at 25 %)

reads run_view.scan(): config.xml 72 KB, modestats.csv 50 KB, scorestats.csv 24 KB, telemetry_live.json 9 KB, telemetry.jsonl WHOLE (2.56 MB by it.300; read_jsonl has a tail parameter nobody passes), _config.json 393 KB, _meta/_run; walks matsim.log incrementally from a saved offset (run_view._read_markers, 16 MB chunks); computes the relaxation verdict; writes _progress.json 7.8 KB atomically. ~3.1 MB of reads per 30 s at the end of a 300-iteration arm, growing ~8.5 KB per iteration

command (run_matsim.py:2088-2103)
java -Xms48g -Xmx48g -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xlog:gc*:file=<run>/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -cp <201-jar signals run stack + .tools/classes> citysim.CitysimSignalsControler config.xml; JFR only under RUN.machine.jfr_profile (false); no other flag - no -XX:ParallelGCThreads, no NUMA, no compressed-oops tuning (48g is above the 32 GB compressed-oops limit, so every reference is 8 bytes)
heap_rule
RUN.machine.heap_floor_gib 15.6 + RUN.machine.heap_per_fraction_gib 87 x 0.25 = 37.35 GiB; refuse_small_heap (run_matsim.py:653) refuses less, announce_heap (:597) prints it ('heap: -Xmx48g against the registry rule's 37.4 GiB' in the launch log); registry default RUN.machine.xmx 18g, the arm overlay 48g
given_vs_peak_arm0
max heap 47,104 MB (Gbl: max. Memory); MemoryObserver high-water 42,719 MB of 1,819 samples (performance.json memory); gc.log (391 Pause Full, 8,586 Pause Young, regex over the whole file this pass): live after a full collection median 23,977 MB, max 29,262 MB (28.6 GiB); by uptime band 23,401 / 26,601 / 25,615 / 26,172 / 22,472 MB medians at 0-20 / 20-40 / 40-60 / 60-80 / 80-110 ks - a plateau from ~it.60, NO slope to the horizon, and the last band (the innovation-off tail) is the lowest; committed heap swung 41,120-47,154 MB under ParallelGC adaptive sizing despite Xms=Xmx; exit: ParOldGen 33.5 GB used 23.0 GB (68 %), Metaspace 51 MB. (9.169 quotes peak 26,863 MB at 22.9 h from a coarser read of the same file; this pass's max is 29,262 MB.)
gc_cost
full 391 x median 2.49 s (max 47.2 s) = 1,447.5 s; young 8,586 x median 101 ms (max 24.2 s) = 1,307.5 s; total 2,755 s = 2.52 % of the 109,255 s JVM uptime - the heap is not the wall
headroom
47.1 GB max heap - 29.3 GB live peak = 17.8 GB of full-GC headroom; JVM working set ~48g + metaspace/threads on a 63.5 GB host beside the harness's Python (the trend reader alone reached 39.8 GB on 14 Sep, 9.169 - which is why one arm at a time and the bounded cache both matter)
was_heap_binding
NO on arm 0 (48g), the F34/F35 probes (live 19.9-20.3 GB) or today's 1 % smoke (4.9 GB live of 16 GB committed under 18g, 12 full collections in 221 s). YES on F33 arm 0 (aborted_20260910T222830_300it_25pct): 14g, 97 iterations, OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space in the replanning of it.98 after 6.5 h + 13.1 h wedged (9.165) - the overlay had inherited the registry's 14g. What now prevents it: refuse_small_heap (37.4 GiB at 25 %), the stall kill at 1800 s (would have cut the 13.1 h wedge), GC log on by default, checkpoints every 25. A 25 % arm at 40g (F32's setting) would have run with ~10.7 GB of headroom over arm 0's live peak - 48g is the right side of the rule on this host and 64g does not fit
slope_check
(29.3 GB at 25 % - 4.9-8.7 GB at 1 %) / 0.24 = 86-102 GiB per unit fraction on the maxima, 63-80 on the medians, against the declared 87: the rule stands; 9.169 deliberately did not re-declare it on one surviving arm

python

post_run_pipeline (run_matsim.py:1750-1846 close_out, :2210-2235; results_store.py:208-277)
1) _run.json + _meta (instant); 2) summarise_run.summarise() in the harness process: ET.iterparse over output/output_events.xml.gz (1.57 GB gz) for departures/arrivals/stuck per mode + the relaxation verdict -> _summary.json/SUMMARY.md; 3) results_store.process(extract=True): mirror the records, then TWO reporter subprocesses - report_mode_ridership.py --trend (every readable iteration: 38 on arm 0 at every-10 trips tables + plans dumps) and --json for the final iteration -> processed/modes_trend.txt, modes_final.json; 4) run.py then shells extract_metrics.py --run -> _metrics.json (trips/legs/schedule/links/counts). fit.py (_fit.json) is NOT in the automatic chain: it is run by calibrate/session code and calls rmr.report() in-process (fit.py:128-132)
measured_on_the_two_results (file mtimes)
F32 arm: _run 23:21:03 -> _summary 23:24:21 (3.3 min events pass) -> modes_trend 23:29:46 (5.4 min, ~32 iterations) -> modes_final 23:30:04 (18 s) -> _metrics 23:30:16 (12 s): 9.2 min all-in. ARM 0: _run 02:44:22 -> _summary 02:48:43 (4.35 min for the 1.57 GB events file) -> and then NOTHING in processed/: results/processed/20260912T202242_300it_25pct/ holds only the records mirrored at 02:48 (no modes_trend.txt, no modes_final.json, no _metrics.json, no _fit.json, no _process_log.txt); the launch log (results/_launch/citysim_run_20260912T202238.log) ends at 'relaxed: True accounting closes: True' 02:48. The --trend subprocess is the reader 9.169 found holding 39.8 GB (the unbounded per-iteration table cache over 38 iterations, ~1 GB per iteration read) - it did not finish. raw/ holds _metrics.json (03:43:13) and _fit.json (03:43:40), written by hand in the forty-sixth session and never mirrored. FINDING: the newest result's findings are NOT in processed/ - _findings_in_processed is False, so trim will refuse to delete the raw bulk (safe), but the store's contract that findings are permanent is unmet for the project's second result
what_reads_the_events_file_and_how_often
per close-out: summarise_run.events_accounting (iterparse, once, 3.3-4.35 min at 25 %). On demand only: report_mode_ridership --truck-stations (regex pass over it.N events, :340-370), replay_events.py, frontage_volumes.py, measure_corridor_composition.py, diagnose_*. extract_metrics.py reads NO events (links from output_links.csv, counts from the trips/legs tables). The ninth report's '3x per close-out' is now 1x in the default chain; the 3x arises only when --truck-stations and fit are also run
trips_legs_reads
iteration_reading.table() decodes a table once per process into a list of csv.DictReader dicts (bounded at CACHE_TABLES 6 since 9.169); extract_metrics.rows() goes through it (extract_metrics.py:123-144), so output_trips/legs are decoded once per extract_metrics process; report_mode_ridership in ITS process decodes them again (a separate subprocess per --trend / --json / fit call): the final-iteration trips table (18 MB gz, 158,442 resident linked trips) + legs (47 MB gz) are decoded 3-4 times per close-out across processes - each ~10-20 s, so <=1.5 min per arm
one_reading_cost
report_mode_ridership.py --run 20260912T202242_300it_25pct --it 300: 20.2 s wall, rc 0, measured this pass (a cold subprocess: registry load + trips + legs + the run's own output_transitSchedule.xml.gz + targets). The viewer now computes exactly this in-process per requested iteration and caches it; a --trend over 38 iterations is ~13 min of CPU if memory stays bounded (before 9.169 it was the 39.8 GB process)
could_one_pass_serve_every_question
yes for the tables: trips + legs + schedule decoded once could serve summarise (departure/arrival counts by mode are in the legs table), extract_metrics, fit and the final reporter in ONE process instead of four; the events file is needed only for stuck/abort accounting (summarise) and the count-station heavy share (--truck-stations), and those two regex/iterparse passes could be one streaming pass. The saving is 3-6 min per arm (<0.4 % of 30 h) - the ninth report's rank 5 - but the memory bound and the 'findings reach processed' contract matter more than the minutes
build_status_board / session_gate
read processed/ and _run.json records only (kilobytes); not a cost

build

finding
performance.json build_timing is the typed string 'none recorded: no producing script writes its wall time into a report or the manifest' (collect_performance.py:371), and that string is FALSE for this repository: src/build/build_timing.py exists (9.158), 27 of 39 builder scripts under src/build/ and cities/newcastle/build/ wrap their main in it (grep 'import build_timing'), and cities/newcastle/data/_build_timing.json (gitignored, outside the hashed set by design - a wall time inside a hashed artefact would churn every manifest hash) holds 12 recorded builders totalling 1,695.7 s: build_activity_chains 1,180.1 s, build_matsim_network 248.8 s, build_matsim_plans 141.6 s, build_matsim_signals 77.6 s, build_population 26.6 s, build_charging_dwell_offsets 9.9 s, build_landuse_parking 4.4 s, build_level_crossings 4.4 s, build_gtfs_extras 1.0 s, build_mode_targets 0.6 s, build_corridor_layers 0.5 s, build_zone_attractions 0.2 s (recorded 10-12 Sep 2026)
what_is_still_unrecorded
the 12 unwrapped scripts include the two that matter for a rebuild: src/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py (assembles the 30 scenario x day run-input sets; re-run 14 Sep for the 250 horizon, 9.169) and src/build/build_manifest.py (hashes 512 files), plus build_data_dictionary.py, normalise_eol.py and the library modules (det_io, gtfs_tools, osm_parse, shape_tools, subpopulations, hts_purpose, asc_fields); cities/newcastle/build/build_era_feeds.py; and the acquisition/mapping steps outside src/build/ - the Overpass harvest in cities/newcastle/extract/ and the pt2matsim schedule mapping (build_scenario_schedules.py IS wrapped but has no record because it has not run since the module landed). Only builders that have RUN since 12 Sep appear, so the file is a partial ledger of the last rebuild, not the cost of a full reproduction
recommendation
(a) collect_performance.py should read cities/<city>/data/_build_timing.json (via src/city.py) and report per-builder seconds and the total, replacing the typed string - the ninth report's rank 6, still open; (b) wrap build_matsim_run_inputs.py, build_manifest.py and the extract adapters in build_timing.timed(); (c) keep the wall times OUT of the manifest and the builders' own _*_report.json (9.158's reason stands) - the right place is exactly where it is, one gitignored file per city, plus a one-line 'total build wall' cell the report reads; (d) a full-reproduction timing needs one clean rebuild from raw, which no session has run since the file existed - that is the measurement, and it is a workstation task, not a CI one

warm start

what_the_launcher_does
run.py --warm-start <dead run dir>: resolve_warm_start (run_matsim.py:165) takes the newest ITERS/it.N/N.plans.xml.gz of a run WITHOUT a _run.json, sets RUN.controler.first_iteration = N; warm_start_overrides (:841) re-derives RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation so the cutoff ITERATION is the parent's (#192); check_warm_compatibility (:237) refuses a different scenario/day/fraction/seed/threads/overrides (xmx still not checked)
what_it_costs_and_saves_on_arm0
checkpoints at it.0, 1, 25 ... 300 (14 plans dumps, 636-1,085 MB each, 12.7 GB): insurance paid ~2,169 s of plans-only milestone wall + ~9 GB over the every-100 setting; a crash is bounded to <= 25 iterations = <= 2.4 h at 346 s plus ~23 min of setup routing on restart; realised value on this arm 0 (it did not die). Not carried on a warm start: the RNG stream, TravelTimeCalculator link times, RidePairingEngine's previous-mobsim realised times, SCATS state, the taxi fleet's refusal history - so a warm-completed arm is a different run (9.76/#75 unruled). Verdict on the 250-iteration horizon

The 250-iteration horizon is reachable at the measured pace and has been executed once: arm 0 of F35 ran iterations 0-249 in 25.64 h of iteration wall (stopwatch.csv) and all 300 in 30.35 h against a 44 h ceiling and a 39.0 h quote, with no stall, no gate and no heap event (391 full collections, 2.5 % of the wall, live peak 29.3 GB under 48g). A pair arm on the declared horizon (cutoff 200, a 49-iteration tail at 262 s instead of 351 s) prices at ~24.5-26.0 h on arm 0's own banded clock and ~30 h at 300; every figure here is for controler f84a8a3a, and the controler on disk is 64bf91ad (#197, the workers hand their detours to the main thread), whose 25 % pace is 'unmeasured - needs a probe arm' (the 1 % smoke moved 50.4 -> 51.0 s, inside the spread; the pricer already refuses to quote on it without one). Where an iteration goes is settled to the second: the mobsim is 236 s (68 %) executing 2.80 M departures of which 2.30 M are walk legs on a 382,734-link network the qsim never saw before F34, replanning is 85 s (24.5 %) and is MATSim's router on 363,818 walk links, and this project's own listeners are 15-17 s (4-5 %) and falling with the taxi refusal count - the 9.168 Java change removed the one large piece that was ours, and nothing that remains halves the iteration: the two levers that could (a plain-link factory for the time-invariant links, a footpath-graph contraction or beeline prune for the router) are network changes that each need a probe arm before they can be priced, threads are saturated, FIFO and teleported walk are refused on correctness, and 10 % is refused by directive. What the measurements buy at zero model cost is bounded and worth taking: ~20 min per arm from every-50 checkpoints, a quote that lands within +-6 % instead of -22 %, and a close-out that finishes - the newest result's findings never reached processed/ because the --trend reader grew to 39.8 GB and the harness logged nothing about it; the cache is bounded now but the extraction has not been re-run, which is the one item on this list that is a correctness item as well as a performance one.

what the comparison says

  • 55 agent-based city projects on 12 platforms; the ladder is 7 / 12 / 26 / 10 / 0 (none / survey shares / road link counts / transit ridership counts / per-mode every mode). The top rung is still empty across the field; this project is the only attempt and reads 2 of 12 inside 10 % at its newest result (arm 0 of F35).
  • Every stored row was inside its horizon and carried; the 40 calls went to 14 open gaps and closed 5 (VSP titles, the TNO candidate, joint trip-length calibration, the wall-time half of run cost, the OpenPaths cell), narrowed 8, and opened 3.
  • The first like-for-like 25 % clock in the field: Kelheim v3.0's own stopwatch, 388 iterations in ~15.5 h (~139 s recurring) for ~120,000 people, against this project's 346 s and 30.35 h for 155,233 persons kept. Heap remains unpublished field-wide.
  • The matsim-scenarios family calibrates mode share by the Rakow & Nagel log-ratio fixed point and matches trip-length distributions by hand-set marginal utilities of travelling per mode (Lausitz, in print), or not at all in the objective (Berlin's script); nobody states a tolerance for distance. This project's walk-length residual (3.74 vs 0.70 km) is a demand-build property the field's score-side levers do not reach.
  • The ASC method note behind matsim.calibration is three pages, CC BY, and identical in form to asc_fixed_point.py; its damping advice ('by a fraction') is the value this project declares on CAL.asc.damping.
  • Barcelona-MATSim (2019) is the library's cleanest holdout count validation - counts untouched by calibration, reported as an occupancy band, misses attributed to port freight and through traffic by link name - and it is the first published bearing on gap 9 with numbers.
  • Rotterdam-The Hague (2025) removes mode choice from MATSim by design and calibrates once outside the loop; its shares are reported with no observed column. It is the newest real-region ActivitySim + MATSim coupling and the survey's second co-simulation row.
  • The MWCOG Ver. 1.1.0 validation memo - the newest per-mode boardings table in the field - is cited but unpublished on every page read; the subcommittee that would table it meets 18 September 2026.

data acquired answer

No comparable agent-based project holds per-mode observed ridership for EVERY mode it simulates. The closest are agency activity-based models - MWCOG Gen3 holds operator boardings for Metrorail, commuter rail and bus from the operators (Ver. 1.0.4 table, with bands), PSRC SoundCast holds per-operator boardings - and the two smartcard rows: Cape Town MyCiTi (AFC boardings from the city's BRT operator, one mode) and Seoul (T-money station boardings/alightings, figures paywalled). AToM Melbourne holds 48 + 48 automatic bike and pedestrian counters from Victoria's open data. Barcelona-MATSim (added this pass) holds 11 entrance count stations from the city council and the EMEF survey, nothing per transit mode; Rotterdam-The Hague states no observed dataset at all. Nobody holds observed counts for taxi, motorbike, bike, walk, bus, rail, tram, ferry and freight at once. This project holds RMS permanent counts (30 calibration stations + holdout), Opal station entries/exits and light-rail trips by stop, bus trips by contract region, HTS shares, BITRE motorcycle registrations and P2P fare arithmetic - and lacks bike/pedestrian counters, per-service bus occupancy in the fit module (BOAM on disk), and a row-level ferry patronage record (the Opal Ferry dataset page read this pass describes Sydney Ferries routes only).

physical fidelity answer

The best-validated rows carry LESS physical fidelity than this project, not more. MWCOG Gen3 (per-mode transit boardings within bands) is a static-assignment agency model - no signals, no dwell, no parking search. Cape Town (R2 0.85 on tap boardings) is MATSim pt on a schedule with hand-tuned capacities and walk penalties, no signals. Barcelona-SUMO (R2 0.81 on 488 stations) ran SUMO's generic actuated controller at 2,035 signals because the city's plans were unavailable, held fixed. Barcelona-MATSim (GEH < 10 on 9 of 11 holdout stations) has imputed capacities and no signals. Kelheim, Berlin and Lausitz run pt on GTFS with walk teleported (Lausitz states beeline 1.3 in print this pass) and no signals in the released scenario. No agent-based project in 55 rows has measured signals, dwell, parking or crossings against a validation figure (confirmed twice, gaps 12 and 13). This project runs SCATS as its published algorithm with transit signal priority, level crossings as timetable closures, priced parking with search time, pt access/egress/transfer walks as network legs (27,765 executed, 0 teleported on arm 0), and a taxi fleet and ride pairing - above the field's fidelity floor on every axis, with no comparator that prices what it buys and its own first fidelity control still one approved arm away.

warm start answer

No comparable MATSim project warm-starts or checkpoints a calibration arm as a stated practice. The platform's only mechanism is a plans-file restart at the checkpoint iteration (MATSim issue #834); matsim-scenarios ship calibrated output plans as input plans; Kelheim v3.0's published 25 % output is one 388-iteration run; Rotterdam-The Hague restarts MATSim from ActivitySim's demand each outer LOS iteration; the calibration scripts (Berlin's calibrate.py, the Rakow method) run each trial as a fresh MATSim run. This project's --warm-start (crash recovery from the newest plans checkpoint, cutoff iteration re-derived) and arm 0's every-25 plan dumps (12 checkpoints, ~50 min of a 30.35 h arm) remain the only stated policy in the survey - and arm 0 did not need it (warm_started_from: null).

Every controllable value declared with units, provenance and a sweep or held-fixed rule (558 fields), every living number pinned to its artefact by a check, twelve modes each monitored on its own basis every tenth iteration - and, unique in this survey, a REGISTRY-ENFORCED refusal to fit a constant over a named missing mechanism (C.asc.rail's departure_requires clause). THIS PASS ADDS A SECOND UNIQUENESS, AND IT IS THE HONEST ONE: the project's _fit.json scores mode shares, absolute link counts, trip-length geometry and vehicle occupancy IN ONE ARTEFACT FROM ONE RUN, names its 32 unscorable targets with reasons, and refuses to call a stopped arm a result. Across 53 surveyed projects, the closest published analogues each hold part of that - AToM validates five observation families but calibrates against one; Tallinn optimises three target families at once but reports no per-mode transit rung; the WFRC framework enumerates every validation summary but states outright that not all of them can be met simultaneously. | 2026-09-14: against the three rows added this pass the position sharpens - Cape Town reaches the tap-data rung for ONE operator with ~25 hand-tuned runs; mobiTopp Stuttgart calibrates trip-length distributions and modal split jointly but by eye; Barcelona runs generic actuated signals at 2,035 intersections on full demand for R2 0.81 on counts and nothing else. None scores more than one observation family with a stated band. | 2026-09-14 (tenth pass): the claim is now made against a RESULT with 2 of 12 inside 10 % rather than 0 - and against 55 rows. The two rows added this pass sharpen it from opposite sides: Barcelona-MATSim (2019) validates on counts it never calibrated on and names the excluded demand behind its two misses, which this project's fit module does for its 32 unscorable targets but not yet for its count outliers; Rotterdam-The Hague (2025) removes mode choice from MATSim altogether so that one calibrator owns it, where this project's twelve constants are scored inside the co-evolutionary loop they must survive.

calibration_method
family
coordinate descent over registry-declared sweeps (unchanged, never run to completion) PLUS, NEW AT THIS HEAD AND NEVER RUN, an implemented ASC log-ratio fixed point - src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py. Read from the source at HEAD 781cf41, not searched.
what_the_source_says
src/calibrate/calibrate.py:508-533 runs coordinate descent: per round, per free parameter, per grid point across that parameter's registry sweep, a FULL MATSim run -> extract_metrics -> fit -> a weighted scalar objective over declared _fit.json components, keeping a point only if it is feasible against the C4 occupancy and trip-length constraints; the round stops when the improvement falls below delta. The search space is DERIVED FROM THE REGISTRY, not listed in the script: a field is free only if it is source=assumed, carries a scalar sweep and is not held_fixed. The six mode constants are held_fixed under DECISIONS.md 8.5 and are therefore unreachable from the loop by construction - so this project has NO log(target/modelled) ASC loop of any kind. The one constant that is solved, asc_car_passenger, is solved in a separate module (solve_asc_ride.py:101-121) by SECANT INTERPOLATION ON log(ride_per_car) against the observed passenger:driver ratio, and is reported as a CONSTRAINT, not an estimate. The loop refuses to fit more parameters than the objective identifies (four independent numbers) and cannot read a holdout row by construction.
objective_evaluations
coordinate descent: calibrate.py:433 computes the budget as sum(len(grid(p, points_per_param)) for p in free) * max_rounds FULL MATSim runs; at 25% an arm reaching iteration 100 cost 7.66 h wall, so a 3-point 3-parameter 2-round search is ~18 arms and ~140 machine hours. THE LOOP HAS NEVER BEEN RUN TO COMPLETION. The ASC fixed point is far cheaper by design - TWO arms settle the contraction question - and is the only one of the two that has an evaluation count small enough to state in advance. Neither has been executed.
convergence_criterion
round-over-round objective improvement < delta

asc_fixed_point_new_this_pass
src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py EXISTS and PROPOSES ONLY; it has NEVER BEEN RUN. It applies delta_i = damping * [ ln(target_i/modelled_i) - ln(target_ref/modelled_ref) ] against car as reference - the same object as the Berry (1994) share inversion and the same expression matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools computes verbatim, with the damping declared on CAL.asc.damping. THREE DESIGN CHOICES ARE UNUSUAL AND WORTH RECORDING: (1) THE TEST IS THE CONTRACTION, NOT THE SHARES - two damped rounds are compared mode by mode, and if |delta| shrinks the residual is a taste that constants will close, while if it does not shrink the deficit is STRUCTURAL and no constant will ever close it. That is a cheap, decisive, published-in-spirit answer to the 'constant or mechanism' question that the agency protocol answers only by ordering. (2) It CANNOT REACH A FROZEN CONSTANT: it reads held_fixed from the registry and refuses, structurally, the way the holdout guard refuses. (3) On heavy rail and light rail the step is marked basis_is_boardings and reported as a PROXY, because the logit inversion is exact only for shares of a common total. ROUND 1 IS PROPOSED OFF THE F31 GATE AND NOT APPLIED: bike -0.5121, bus -0.2301, ferry +0.6713, light rail +0.4143.
read_against_the_field_this_pass
Two published methods now bracket this project's loop and both were read this pass. (1) Chen, Prakash, Lima de Azevedo & Ben-Akiva (2020, TR-C 119:102650) names this project's coordinate descent for what it is: 'myopic heuristics in the sense that they do not consider the fundamental inter-dependencies among choice-models and do not have a systematic way to adjust model parameters' - and their non-myopic alternative calibrates precisely this project's target set at once (activity shares, mode shares, mode-specific OD flows, mode-specific sensor counts). (2) The WFRC/RSG ActivitySim framework publishes New ASC = Old ASC + ln(Target Proportion / Model Proportion) verbatim - the exact expression in asc_fixed_point.py - inside a CYCLIC protocol over model components, and states plainly that 'It is typically the case that not all calibration and validation targets can be achieved simultaneously.' | 2026-09-11 (third bracket): POLARIS's published procedure is the same cyclic ASC-by-purpose update, TIERED by iteration so that 'network state' can 'adapt to this change in demand' before the next tier is touched, with counts and speeds explicitly outside the calibrated set ('can only be minimally calibrated'). MATSim-NYC calibrated NO demand constants at all - its nested logit was estimated on RHTS + TLC/FHV/Citi Bike records and converted analytically - and spent its six SPSA iterations on twelve link-CAPACITY factors instead, which is the opposite allocation to this project's.

warm_start
--warm-start <dead run dir> exists in src/run/run_matsim.py: it resumes from a dead run's newest plans checkpoint, records warm_started_from, and RE-DERIVES RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation so the innovation cutoff ITERATION is the parent's (the pinned jar's first + f x (last - first) had moved it 240 -> 260 at N = 100, #192). It is crash recovery, not a bit-identical continuation. Arm 0 of F35 dumps plans every 25 iterations for exactly this reason (the F33 arm that died at 98 had checkpoints at it.0 and it.1 only). This matches the platform's own answer (MATSim issue #834: restart AT the checkpoint iteration from its post-replanning plans); the platform has no finer mechanism, and the interval is the whole trade.     calibration_tooling
    Three named routes, all read this pass: (1) matsim.calibration in matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools - an ASCCalibrator driving an Optuna study, whose update is literally log(z_i) - log(m_i) - (log(z_0) - log(m_0)), i.e. the classic ASC fixed-point loop normalised on a fixed reference mode, with a pluggable learning-rate scheduler and a TerminationCondition dataclass whose check_termination carries "# TODO: not used yet"; (2) Cadyts, a Bayesian count calibration that adjusts NO parameter and instead adds a utility bonus so agents select the plans matching observed counts; (3) opdyts (Flotterod, TR-B 2017), which approximates point equilibria of the mobsim/scoring/replanning loop, with a Berlin mode-constant example. See calibration_methods. | 2026-09-14: the METHOD NOTE behind route (1) is now read in full - Rakow & Nagel, 'Automated calibration of alternative specific constants in agent based transport models', TU Berlin, June 2024, doi 10.14279/depositonce-20593, CC BY 4.0, three pages. Verbatim: 'Perform a simulation run until convergence and collect all relevant trips. Let z_i be the reference mode share for mode i and m_i the simulated mode share. One ASC always has to be fixed (usually to 0); otherwise, the solution is not unique ... asc_i + ln z_i - ln m_i - (ln z_0 - ln m_0) ... Perform more simulation runs while updating asc_i by delta_i for all modes i, except i = 0 after each run. This is done until simulated mode shares are sufficiently close to the reference mode shares.' Proof given for two alternatives under fixed utilities; discussion: 'The proof assumes that utilities remain constant during simulation runs, which is often not the case ... it is recommended to adjust the update step delta_i by a fraction. This fraction can be modified based on the difference between simulated and reference mode shares.' No run count, no scenario, no fit figure, no distance term in the note; the tooling's ASCDistCalibrator adds distance-group constants with the same update. The idea is credited to Gunnar Floetteroed. This is the exact expression in this project's asc_fixed_point.py, and it is cited as the calibration tool by the Rotterdam-The Hague row (Li et al. 2025).
    carried_to
    2026-09-14
    restart_mechanism
    NO checkpoint/resume exists in the platform. The developer answer (Marcel Rieser, matsim-code-examples issue #834, 12 Dec 2022, read via api.github.com this pass): 'The plans in "it200/200.plans.xml.gz" are the plans after replanning, but before mobsim, in iteration 200. So you can use those to resume at iteration 200 (it should generate the same events file like the first run), and then continue with iteration 201.' and 'If you use the plans file of iteration 200, start the new run also with iteration 200.' ... 'The first iteration of a run never does replanning.' So a resume is a plans-file restart AT the checkpoint iteration, and only where a plans dump exists (writePlansInterval); everything since the last dump is lost. Memory rule of thumb from the same repository's issue #189: 'typically... around 100KB per agent. That is 1 GB per 10k agents' (mrieser, 2019-08-20); a ~1M-agent, 250k-link scenario needed 60-90 GB actual (mrieser); JVM total is ~25% above the reported heap (josiekre).
    updated_this_pass
    Rakow & Nagel 2024 read in full: the ASC fixed-point note behind matsim.calibration, formula and damping advice verbatim

Class OUT unchanged.None.Two 2025-2026 results now bracket this lane. On the optimistic side, GATSim integrates LLM-powered generative agents - hierarchical memory, multi-modal retrieval, planning, reactive and reflection processes, diverse socioeconomic profiles and lifelong learning - into an urban mobility environment, and reports validation at microscopic and macroscopic levels, claiming agents 'perform competitively with human annotators in role-playing scenarios' while 'naturally producing realistic macroscopic traffic patterns'; its abstract states no accuracy figure, no real city and no cost per agent-day. On the sceptical side, the first systematic evaluation against observed mobility (2026) measures AgentSociety and CitySim over Greater Paris (3,337 residents, 7 days) and Shanghai (58,502 users, 10 days) and separates 'face validity' from 'objective mobility realism': AgentSociety's travel-distance error is a Wasserstein distance of 14.83 plus or minus 0.35 km and CitySim's 7.53 plus or minus 1.67 km, with origin-destination similarity at a common-part-of-commuters of 0.138 plus or minus 0.018; trip-duration error is 24.41 plus or minus 0.24 minutes and dwell-time error 3.96 plus or minus 0.12 hours, against reference-sample variability of 0.29 minutes and 0.26 hours. Activity PROPORTIONS come out well (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.0296) while activity SEQUENCES do not (0.1125), and mobility diversity is 'unstable across default prompting configurations'. The finding to carry: LLM agents reproduce qualitative mobility laws and aggregate activity mixes, and miss individual spatial behaviour by one to two orders of magnitude more than sampling error.https://arxiv.org/html/2606.138352026-09-08

Class PARTIAL unchanged.light_rail -73.9 moving AWAY across 300 iterations is a non-fixed-point reading the drift tolerance cannot see because the tram is 1,224 boardings on a 154,347-person sample.MATSim's mobsim/scoring/replanning loop is a Monte-Carlo co-evolutionary search, not a solved fixed point, and its own authors say so. Floetteroed's statement of the position is the clearest available: the assignment relies on approximate minimisation of an EQUILIBRIUM GAP measuring, for every agent, how much that agent could improve its score by changing its plan if all other agents kept theirs; 'the gap is always non-negative and zero at a (possibly non-existing) Nash equilibrium', and the method 'aims to reduce the gap in subsequent MATSim iterations, steering the simulation process towards a state that has a low gap, and hence may be deemed to be near an equilibrium point'. He names the reproducible computation of point equilibria as 'the single most important advantage' of the traditional four-step / static-assignment model - an advantage MATSim does not have by default - and supplies the emulation and greedo contribs that add gap minimisation to the loop, illustrated on a multimodal Greater Stockholm scenario with all-day route, departure-time and mode choice. The wider theory agrees: MATSim targets a STOCHASTIC user equilibrium (minimum PERCEIVED cost) rather than a Nash equilibrium; best-response dynamics carry no convergence guarantee, though if they converge they converge to an equilibrium. No published convergence rate exists for a multimodal MATSim scenario: relaxation is asserted by observation, not proved.https://ethz.ch/content/dam/ethz/special-interest/baug/ivt/ivt-dam/events/2023/09/05/abstracts/Floetteroed_MUM_2023.pdf2026-09-08

Class OUT unchanged.None.An architecture that avoids the outer loop entirely: estimate the utility parameters INSIDE the simulation, against a subpopulation of real survey respondents whose observed plans are pinned. The MATSim planParamCalibration extension does exactly that - a designated subpopulation carries its surveyed plan under the KeepLastSelected strategy so those plans are the ground truth, the remaining agents generate alternatives by the ordinary strategies, and CMA-ES maximises a logit-like log-likelihood over the planCalcScore parameters (mode constants, marginal utility of travelling, of distance and of money, daily monetary constants, typical and minimal activity durations, line-switch, waiting, late-arrival and early-departure terms) at each MATSim iteration, writing the result back into the config for the next one. It stops on a designated iteration or on convergence, the default being an average estimated difference below 0.001. Tested on a 2023 street-interview trip-diary survey plus mobile-location commuting arrays at 100 m grid accuracy, the maximum log-likelihood is stable over twenty MATSim iterations and essentially unchanged whether the calibration population is respondents alone or respondents plus 100k, 300k, 600k or one million commuting records - the claimed proof that the estimator is auto-adaptive to population scale. The price of the architecture is exactly the data an aggregate-only city lacks: the likelihood's observations are unit-record plans.https://www.matsim.org/conferences/mum2024/presentations/MUM2024_Lu.pdf2026-09-08

Class PARTIAL unchanged.Every deviation; the loop has no finished evaluation to its name.Calibrating a microsimulation is a black-box, stochastic, expensive simulation-based optimisation problem, and the published methods separate by how many simulation evaluations they can afford. SPSA (simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation) is the field's workhorse because it costs only two simulation evaluations per gradient estimate whatever the dimension, and W-SPSA extends it with a weight matrix; but it is built for asymptotic guarantees rather than early termination, and under a small budget it barely moves - on a Salt Lake City origin-destination calibration of order thirty thousand dimensions SPSA took the vehicle-count nRMSE from 120% to 117% over fifteen simulation iterations, while a metamodel method reached 32%. Evolutionary strategies (CMA-ES, xNES) and finite-difference gradient approximation (FDSA, SPSA) are what the MATSim/eqasim calibration framework boptx implements. The cross-entropy method is a Monte-Carlo importance-sampling search and is the most expensive family: one published SUMO calibration of a three-intersection model spent 98,304 simulation evaluations. Bayesian optimisation over a surrogate is the current answer for a small budget (see the surrogate row). The field states its own constraint plainly: computational budgets in the literature are 'one to two orders of magnitude lower than the problem dimension', and general-purpose algorithms 'are designed for asymptotic performance guarantees and are not designed to be terminated with such few function evaluations'.https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.113922026-09-08

Class PARTIAL unchanged.taxi and bike share one HTS 'Other' cell, so one of the two deviations is not independent evidence.A parameter set is identified only if distinct parameter values produce distinguishable outputs on the targets you actually hold, and the simulation-calibration literature is explicit that when a model is over-parametrised relative to its targets, 'non-identifiability can arise, making it theoretically impossible to locate the true parameter value'. The published remedy is not a better optimiser but a different answer: report an ELIGIBILITY SET - the set of all parameter values whose simulated outputs match the data - constructed to carry rigorous frequentist guarantees, extended to multivariate outputs by a feature-extraction-then-aggregation construction. The counting rule underneath is what binds a mode-share calibration: K shares that sum to one contain K-1 independent numbers, so scoring twelve modelled modes against a five-mode survey does not supply twelve independent targets. The only way to buy identifiability for more parameters is to add targets of a DIFFERENT kind - link counts, boardings, trip-length and duration distributions - not more shares of the same total. In dynamic OD calibration, 'the first formulation estimates the whole set of time-dependent OD matrices SIMULTANEOUSLY for the entire time period in one calibration round. The second formulation estimates and calibrates OD matrices SEQUENTIALLY one at a time for each time frame. Most optimization-based studies have used the simultaneous approach, since the available sequential methods may lose accuracy due to giving up some information in the transition between time frames' - while the simultaneous form 'is incapable of handling a stream of data for real-time or online demand calibration'. The same paper states the bind that makes the choice matter at all: 'this optimization problem is underdetermined for large-scale networks since the number of roads with traffic measurement is usually several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of all roads in the network', and it names the standard architecture as BI-LEVEL - an upper-level discrepancy minimisation over an inner assignment that must be re-solved at every candidate, where 'performing several DTAs for each optimization task demand considerable computational resources'. In DTA practice the sequential form is supply first and then demand with the supply held fixed; the reported weakness of decomposing is that the stages need not be internally consistent, because each stage's assumed input is not the other stage's output.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.173152026-09-09

Jakob and Blume set it out: with a weighted sum, 'by varying the weights, any point of a convex Pareto front can be obtained... On the other hand, it is possible that parts of the Pareto front cannot be found in case of a non-convex problem... the part between points A and B of the Pareto front cannot be obtained for any weights. The counterweight is cost: 'the computational effort to determine all or at least most of the Pareto front increases significantly with the number of conflicting objectives', and the paper's framing is that the real-world question arises 'where either more than four objectives have to be considered, or the same type of task is repeated again and again with only minor modifications'. Which share is validated is still a decision.MATSim's iterative loop is not stationary while innovation runs: its own terminology page states that 'as long as innovation is still switched on in MATSim (new routes, new times, ...), the result is not truly stationary', and that once innovation is disabled 'the result is indeed a stationary process, but limited to the set of plans that every agent has at that point in time'. The selection protocol before the cutoff 'resembles a MNL choice model', P(i|C) = exp(mu S_i)/sum exp(mu S_j) with mu = brainExpBeta, and the chapter notes that BestPlanSelector is the same selector with an infinite mu. So the pre-cutoff share is a logit-dispersed mixture over each agent's remembered plans and the post-cutoff share is the same population collapsed toward its arg-max: switching innovation off changes the estimator, not only the amount of search. Assignment theory says the same thing from the other side - a low dispersion parameter concentrates flow on the perceived-best alternative and the pattern approaches deterministic user equilibrium, which is the classic 'unrealistic route concentration' that stochastic user equilibrium was introduced to cure. The efficiency loss of that concentration is bounded and modest on real networks - a data-driven estimate for Eastern Massachusetts puts the price of anarchy near 1.30, and other empirical work finds it close to 1 in both light and heavy traffic - so an equilibrium being reached is no guarantee that it resembles the observed day, which is itself a non-equilibrium average.https://matsim.org/docs/userguide/terminology.html2026-09-10

Class OUT unchanged.light_rail -73.9 against bus -15.8 is the sign the literature's 5-15 % rail bonus (Scherer & Dziekan 75 % tram preference at equal service) would move; no arm has carried either switch.Across the comparative literature a rail vehicle attracts more riders than a bus offering the same travel time, frequency and walk distance: transport models find 5-15 % higher expected ridership for rail than for bus with similar characteristics, and Scherer and Dziekan measured a 'psychological rail factor' - a stated preference for rail at equal service - of 63 % for regional train and 75 % for tram against bus. The European review by de Jong and Gunn (2001), as tabulated by Litman, gives car-kilometres with respect to fuel price -0.16 short term and -0.26 long term (commuting -0.12 / -0.23), and car-kilometres with respect to travel time -0.20 short term and -0.74 long term; Goodwin (1996) gives urban-road vehicle travel with respect to travel time -0.27 short run and -0.57 long run. Litman's synthesis states the scaling explicitly: a -0.1 short-run elasticity of vehicle travel with respect to fuel price reflects a -0.3 long-run elasticity, which reflects about -1.2 with respect to total vehicle costs, because most vehicle costs (depreciation, financing, insurance, registration, residential parking) are fixed and short-run effects are about a third of long-run ones. Brons, Nijkamp, Pels and Rietveld's meta-analysis of gasoline-demand price elasticities (158 estimates) finds the demand response driven mainly by fuel efficiency and car ownership and to a lesser degree by mileage per car, with a long-run estimate about -0.46 for total fuel demand. On what a driver actually prices, the classic Transportation paper 'Perceived and actual costs of operating cars' finds the modal split consistent with drivers perceiving petrol costs only, which is why mode-choice models price car by a marginal per-kilometre cost rather than by full cost of ownership.https://www.vtpi.org/elasticities.pdf2026-09-14
H12HHabit, inertia and satisficing: does the agent re-optimise every day, or stick until a threshold is crossed?PARTIALRe-read at b8f89ff (14 Sep 2026): the registry dump (558 fields, value/source/matsim_param/consumer/inert_at), python src/registry/check_hardcoding.py (TOTAL 0; section 1: 0 unwired + 4 declared-ahead; section 2: 0; section 7: 150 of 150 bound fields reach the config, 3 shipped at the off value), CitysimControler.java binding lines, and git diff 780c4c2..b8f89ff (no file this row cites changed unless stated). Habit as a utility term: none - grep 'habit|inertia' over cities/newcastle/registry/*.json and src/java/citysim/*.java finds only prose (E13). Habit as machinery: IN - RUN.replanning.weights ChangeExpBeta 0.7 / ReRoute 0.15 / SubtourModeChoice 0.1 / TimeAllocationMutator 0.05 (RUN_execution.json, bound), RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation 0.8 (literature, sweep 0.7-0.9), RUN.replanning.max_agent_plan_memory 8 (literature, sweep 3-10), RUN.replanning.plan_selector_for_removal WorstPlanSelector (assumed, categorical over MATSim's five, bound replanning.planSelectorForRemoval; SelectRandom the control, unrun), RUN.replanning.score_msa_representation absent (consumer build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1164). Measured: the choice set closes inside the first 30 iterations for every mode but pt (ride 5/17, bike 7/16, walk 7/14, car 8/16, taxi 10/27; pt 123/233 on the F32 result) and the cutoff snap on arm 0 is car +1.683 pp - a satisficing dynamic whose parameters are declared and whose day-to-day switching rate is compared with no observation. Class PARTIAL (machinery in, term out, rate unvalidated).Every scored mode through selection: the board's open question is why convergence makes the fit worse (planned car 62.26 % at it.100 -> 66.94 % at it.300 on arm 0), and habit-as-machinery is exactly where that lives - the selector, the memory and the cutoff decide which remembered plan wins. Bears on car +9.6, bike +201.6 (28 % of agents hold a bike plan and the winner is kept), taxi +131.4. The declared controls (SelectRandom, at_innovation_cutoff MSA) are the two arms that test it; no observation of a day-to-day switching rate exists in the package to validate against.Habit is one of the two strongest predictors of the mode a person uses, and it is a MEASURED effect, not a residual. Three meta-analyses put the pooled correlation between a habit measure and the travel mode used at r+ = 0.50 (Gardner & Abraham 2008), r+ = 0.42 (Lanzini & Khan 2017, 58 primary studies) and r = 0.47 (Hoffmann et al. 2017), against an averaged pooled car-use-intention correlation of r+ = 0.83 in Lanzini & Khan; the review of reviews that collects them (Javaid, Creutzig & Bren d'Amour 2020) notes the differences between the meta-analyses exceed their confidence intervals. In discrete-choice terms inertia is the tendency to stick with the past choice even when another alternative becomes more appealing: Cherchi & Manca (2011, Transportation 38:679-695) test eight specifications on an RP/SP dataset with a mixed logit and find a significant, mode-specific inertia that weakens with learning across the SP experiments; Cantillo, Ortuzar & Williams (2007, Transportation Science) model it as a randomly distributed inertia THRESHOLD with serial correlation. The route-choice literature measures the same thing as an INDIFFERENCE BAND: travellers do not switch unless the saving exceeds a threshold (Mahmassani & Liu 1999), and Zhu & Levinson (2016, Transportation) estimate lognormal bands on 78 GPS subjects around the Minneapolis I-35W bridge replacement, which explains why the new bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving predicted. Satisficing (Simon 1957) is the general form - search stops at a satisfactory alternative - and boundedly rational user equilibrium (Di & Liu 2016 review) is the assignment that follows from it. The magnitudes the field reports are correlations and thresholds, not a utility constant; a simulator represents habit either as a state-dependent term (past mode in the utility), as a switching threshold, or - as MATSim does - as a selection rule over remembered plans.https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aba0322026-09-14
F6FTravel-time reliability and route switching: the reliability ratio and the indifference band in route choicePARTIALRe-read at b8f89ff (14 Sep 2026): the registry dump (558 fields, value/source/matsim_param/consumer/inert_at), python src/registry/check_hardcoding.py (TOTAL 0; section 1: 0 unwired + 4 declared-ahead; section 2: 0; section 7: 150 of 150 bound fields reach the config, 3 shipped at the off value), CitysimControler.java binding lines, and git diff 780c4c2..b8f89ff (no file this row cites changed unless stated). Route choice prices mean time only: RUN.routing.routing_randomness 3.0 (literature, sweep 0-5, bound routing.routingRandomness), ReRoute 0.15 in RUN.replanning.weights, RUN.travel_time.bin_size_s 300; no field named reliability, variance or indifference band reaches the car router (grep 'reliab|variance|indifference' over cities/newcastle/registry: only C.time_weights.beta_reliability, which is the PT boarding term of E12, ServiceQualityScoring.java:122, shipped absent). The switching rate is a declared strategy weight compared with no observation. Class PARTIAL (mean-time route choice with declared randomness; no reliability term, no band).Little on the current board directly: no mode's deviation is attributed to road route choice. Indirectly car +9.6 via congestion pattern and the crossing closures (E24). Its value is as a stated limitation for the P5 scenario comparisons, where a tram-priority or lane-take scenario changes reliability more than mean time.Reliability enters route choice as a second attribute beside mean time, and the field's summary statistic is the RELIABILITY RATIO - the value of a unit of standard deviation over the value of a unit of mean travel time. Carrion & Levinson (2012, TR-A 46(4):720-741) review and meta-analyse the estimates and attribute their spread to measurement (which dispersion measure, SP versus RP, self-reported versus GPS times). The same authors' Minneapolis before-and-after study of the I-35W bridge (39 subjects with complete data, 78 GPS observations) shows how far the ratio moves with measurement alone: 1.30 (mean/SD) and 1.60 (median/SD) on SELF-REPORTED times against 0.42 and 0.77 on GPS-MEASURED times, and 0.83 / 0.39 on the mean-to-90th-percentile measure - a ratio above 1 with perceived times and below 1 with measured ones. Route SWITCHING is boundedly rational: travellers keep their usual route until the saving exceeds an indifference band (Mahmassani & Liu 1999; Zhu & Levinson 2016 estimate lognormal bands on the same 78-subject GPS panel and use them to explain why the replaced bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving implied). For a simulator this means (a) a reliability term in route cost needs a measured day-to-day time variance per link, which a single-day equilibrium simulation does not produce, and (b) the switching rate of the route-choice strategy is itself a behavioural parameter.https://findingspress.org/article/8330-uncovering-the-influence-of-commuters-perception-on-the-reliability-ratio2026-09-14

whatholdsneedsriskgap
.claude/settings.json SessionStartruns four shell commands with the session's full permissions on every session start: sets user.name/user.email to a hardcoded identity (65392157+praneetdhoolia@users.noreply.github.com), commit.gpgsign false, core.hooksPath, the branch reminder, and session_gate.py --digest (which shells out to git, gh and python)the identity pin is deliberate (the attribution rule) but it means every commit from any operator of this checkout is attributed to one person, and --digest calls gh with whatever token the shell holds; nothing here needs write access beyond .git/config, and nothing here has morelow; a compromised session_gate.py would run at every start with the operator's credentials - the file is tracked and reviewed like any other—
.claude/settings.json PreToolUse on Bash (two hooks) and on the two GitHub-MCP PR toolsreads every Bash tool payload; gate-pr-on-docs.sh runs three python checks when the payload contains gh pr create|edit or the MCP PR tool names; both exit 2 to denyonly read; they hold nothing more. The matcher on Bash means every Bash call pays two shell spawns (grep over the payload); they self-scope correctly (block-session-ref-in-gh-pr.sh:18, gate-pr-on-docs.sh:24-27)—a PR opened from the GitHub web UI or gh outside the harness is ungated; the doc gates in CI catch it after the fact
.githooks/commit-msgrewrites the commit message (strips the session-link lines); set -euo pipefail; activated by core.hooksPath at session start onlyexactly this; outside a Claude session the hook is inactive unless the operator sets core.hooksPath themselves (the server-side workflow is the backstop for PR bodies, and nothing backstops a commit made outside the harness)——
.github/workflows/test.yml (9 jobs)permissions: contents: read at the top; the four pip install steps fetch from PyPI at pinned versions (no hashes); actions pinned by SHAread only; holds read only. Correct——
.github/workflows/strip-session-ref.ymlpull-requests: write on pull_request (opened/edited/reopened); runs gh pr edit --body-file - with the repo token when the body matches; no checkoutwrite on pull-requests is the minimum for its job; it acts on same-repo PRs only (a fork PR's token would be read-only, so it would fail closed); the edited event it triggers no-ops (idempotent by the grep guard at :104)low; the body text is only ever passed through sed, never executed—
